clinicalPearls: In d-transposition the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle, so the systemic and pulmonary circulations run in parallel rather than in series.
It is a leading cause of cyanosis presenting in the newborn period, often in an otherwise well-grown, term infant.
Survival depends on mixing between the two parallel circuits through a patent foramen ovale, atrial or ventricular septal defect, or the ductus arteriosus.
Cyanosis is typically profound and, unlike many respiratory causes, does not improve substantially with supplemental oxygen.
A prostaglandin infusion is started to maintain ductal patency and improve intercirculatory mixing while the infant is stabilised.
Balloon atrial septostomy may be performed to enlarge the atrial communication and improve mixing when cyanosis is severe.
Chest radiograph may show an egg-on-a-string cardiac silhouette with a narrow mediastinum, though this is not always present.
Echocardiography confirms the discordant great-artery connections, defines associated defects, and maps the coronary arteries before surgery.
The arterial switch operation, restoring normal ventriculoarterial connections, is the definitive repair and is performed in the neonatal period.
reference.pathophysiology: Abnormal division of the truncus arteriosus results in the aorta connecting to the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery to the left ventricle. As a consequence, deoxygenated systemic venous blood is pumped back to the body and oxygenated pulmonary venous blood is returned to the lungs, forming two separate parallel circuits. Life is only possible if oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix through a communication at the atrial, ventricular, or ductal level. Inadequate mixing produces severe systemic hypoxaemia and progressive metabolic acidosis, which worsens as the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale close after birth.
additionalDifferentials: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography to confirm ventriculoarterial discordance, mixing sites, and coronary anatomy
Hyperoxia test showing little rise in oxygenation with supplemental oxygen (suggesting a cardiac cause)
Chest radiograph looking for an egg-on-a-string silhouette
Blood gas to assess hypoxaemia and acidosis
Pulse oximetry, including pre- and post-ductal comparison
redFlags: Severe cyanosis in a newborn that fails to improve with supplemental oxygen
Rapid deterioration and acidosis as the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale close, restricting mixing
Duct-dependent collapse before prostaglandin is established
Worsening metabolic acidosis indicating inadequate systemic oxygen delivery
Inadequate intercirculatory mixing requiring urgent septostomy
reference.prognosis: With prompt stabilisation and an arterial switch operation in the neonatal period, most children do well with good long-term function, though follow-up is required for coronary, valve, and great-artery complications. Without intervention the condition is rapidly fatal.
pitfalls: Attributing severe neonatal cyanosis to lung disease and delaying cardiac evaluation because oxygen does not help
Failing to start prostaglandin promptly, allowing the ductus to close and mixing to fail
Overlooking the need to enhance mixing (septostomy) in a critically hypoxaemic infant
Assuming a normal chest radiograph excludes the diagnosis
Not mapping coronary anatomy before surgical planning
management: Commence a prostaglandin infusion at presentation to maintain ductal patency and improve intercirculatory mixing during stabilisation
Perform balloon atrial septostomy to enlarge the atrial communication and improve mixing when cyanosis remains severe
Correct metabolic acidosis and hypoxaemia with supportive measures, including mechanical ventilation and inotropic support as required
Undertake the arterial switch operation in the neonatal period as the definitive corrective repair, with careful coronary artery transfer
Manage within a specialist paediatric cardiology and cardiac surgery multidisciplinary team
Provide lifelong cardiology follow-up for coronary, neo-aortic valve and great-artery complications after repair
